newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Dutch soccer clubs line up for bourse kick-off.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Dutch soccer clubs line up for bourse kick-off.

text.p: English soccer clubs may be rushing headlong to the London stock market but Dutch clubs are waiting to bag lucrative television rights before taking the plunge on the Amsterdam exchange.
The pragmatic Dutch approach to what is widely regarded as the inevitable corporatisation of the world's most popular sport is in stark contrast to Britain's Klondike-like dash for cash.

"As more and more money goes into the game in Britain, it will put pressure on European clubs to match it," said Tony Fraher, chief executive of Singer & Friedlander Investment Funds, which recently launched a new Football Fund for investors.
Top clubs in Germany, Italy and Denmark have also indicated that they are considering stock market listings.

Fraher said that a recent court case in the Netherlands, which brought closer the possibility of clubs themselves negotiating big-money TV rights to their home matches, would be very good news for the clubs.
"Television is the key. It not only gives clubs pay-per-view revenues, but also advertising revenues, and it will increase their merchandising abilities on a European scale."
CLUBS KEEN TO MAKE TV DEALS

Currently, the Dutch soccer association KNVB negotiates TV deals for all clubs on a collective basis, but this is about to change with the clubs, who are discussing setting up an elite premier league, keen to cut their own TV deals.

Economic Affairs Minister Hans Wijers, drawn into the affair after the collapse of cable broadcaster Sport 7, has signalled his support for KNVB to act as broker for individual clubs seeking to win TV deals.

Current league leaders PSV Eindhoven, which began life in 1913 as a works club for staff at electronics giant Philips Electronics NV, look set to lead the assault on the Dutch bourse, but not in the immediate future.
Chairman Hans van Raay said PSV's existing structure as a small, closed association did not lend itself to a listing.
"So we don't expect anything to go ahead in the short-term."
The club has said it would expect to be quoted by 2005 in a bid to secure its financial future and keep pace with the rapidly changing soccer world.
PSV is likely to abolish its present structure and turn into a private company with a limited number of major shareholders who would be given grandstand seats in lieu of a cash dividend.
"Football is becoming increasingly international. You need capital to compete successfully with big clubs elsewhere and the stock market offers the best way to raise it," Van Raay said.
AJAX NOT PLANNING LISTING YET

But it will be some time before die-hard fans of former European champions Ajax Amsterdam, this small soccer-mad country's most prestigious sporting brand name, will be able to buy a stake in idols Jari Litmanen or Marc Overmars.
Ajax executives have said that the club's move to a new, rented super-stadium means they don't need extra cash.
"A listing doesn't make sense for us at the moment, but things are always changing. We might be more interested in five years' time," Maarten Oldenhof told Quote magazine last year.
Ajax treasurer Aad van Os is quoted as saying a listing is possible in the long term and probably in conjunction with a move to a possible European "super-league".
The Amsterdam stock exchange has also welcomed the idea of top clubs joining the market, boosting publicity and adding to market turnover.
"I can imagine many investors might see such shares as a fun way to add to their portfolios," a spokesman said.

At the other end of the Dutch soccer spectrum, second division leaders ADO Den Haag plan a private share issue to raise 10 million guilders ($5.3 million) as a prelude to a market listing within five years.

"As league leaders, there's a good chance we'll be in the top flight next season and, if we are to compete with the big boys, we'll need capital. It's that simple," club chairman John van Ringelenstein said in a note on the club's Internet site.
Similarly, premier division strugglers AZ Alkmaar have said they want to raise cash from stakeholders to fund a new stadium.
The trend mirrors recent activity in England where Newcastle United are leading a host of lesser clubs towards the stock market, cashing in on the game's increasing popularity.
English champions Manchester United floated in 1991 and, after a few share price wobbles, are now among the top 250 listed companies in Britain, worth over 460 million pounds ($746 million).

Observers believe the closer links between football and finance will force changes in club boardrooms, altering the role of club chairman from local fan and wealthy benefactor to market-oriented businessman.
"(Team) managers will be trained and the boardroom will become divorced from what happens on the pitch...apart from having to put up money to buy players," Fraher said.
"Nor does it matter who the shareholders are as long as they don't interfere with what goes on on the pitch. They should run the club as a business."
($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
($ = 1.889 Dutch Guilders)
